records.name: Ankara
records.current_summary: Ankara is the administrative core of what the country's leading LGBTI rights organisation — reporting from its capital launch event in 2025 — documented as hostility turned into explicit state policy: presidency-centred targeting, the family ministry as implementing body, broadcast and platform censorship, an LGBTI organisation closed, six violations of the right to life (three recorded as hate-motivated) with trans people most affected, and no official hate-crime statistics in existence. A leaked October 2025 judicial package would add up to three years' imprisonment for conduct contrary to biological sex and its promotion, and bar gender-affirming care below age 25.  The capital hosts the machinery that drafts and enforces those measures; nothing on record shows local countervailing protection, and the same courts and ministries that field the report operate here.

sources.claim: National-framework source (applies country-wide; the package is drafted and enforced by institutions operating in Ankara): HRW (29 Oct 2025) reports the leaked draft “11th Judicial Package” would amend the Turkish penal code to criminalise conduct deemed contrary to biological sex and general morality with up to three years’ prison, participation in same-sex engagement or marriage ceremonies with up to four years, and would raise the minimum age for gender-affirming care including surgery from 18 to 25 with mandatory permanent infertility and repeated evaluations at government-approved hospitals; healthcare professionals performing such interventions would face fines and up to seven years in prison, trans people receiving deemed-illegal care up to three years, and courts could order pretrial detention. Fifteen LGBT groups and the Turkish Medical Association opposed the draft.

National-framework monitoring report (the institutions it names — the presidency, the Ministry of Family — operate in Ankara): Kaos GL’s annual report (“The Year of the Family: A Major Siege Against LGBTI+ People”, launched in 2025) finds LGBTI+ hostility became explicit state policy — hostility centered on the presidency, the Ministry of Family as implementing ministry, broadcasts censored and artistic events cancelled or banned, and an LGBTI+ association closed for the first time in years with criminal cases opened against 11 of its members. It documents six violations of the right to life (three recorded as hate-motivated), trans people the most affected, a sharp rise in torture and ill-treatment violations (89 versus 51 the previous year), and notes the state keeps no official hate-crime statistics.

flags: standing gubernatorial ban on public LGBTI activities (2017-2019 legacy)

records.name: Gaziantep
records.current_summary: Gaziantep sits fully under the national framework with no documented local divergence in either direction: the leaked October 2025 judicial package would criminalise conduct contrary to biological sex and its promotion (up to three years) and restrict gender-affirming care to age 25 and above, while the 2025 national rights report documents hostility as explicit state policy — presidency-centred targeting, censorship, an organisation closed, six violations of the right to life with trans people most affected, and no official protection statistics at all.  Nothing in the record shows this province offering either special danger beyond, or protection beneath, that national baseline; a visibly trans visitor's exposure is the national one, locally enforced.

sources.claim: Human Rights Watch (29 Oct 2025): a leaked '11th Judicial Package' would amend the penal and civil codes with articles threatening LGBT people — behaviour 'contrary to biological sex and general morality' and its 'promotion' (up to three years' prison, amending the indecent-acts provision); sharp restrictions on gender-affirming care (minimum age 25, onerous eligibility); potential charges against trans people, care providers, civil-society organisations and journalists; justified as protecting 'the family and public morals'.

Wikipedia's country page on LGBT rights in Turkey is the framework under which Gaziantep stands, matching this record's premise that the province sits fully under the national baseline: homosexuality has not been a criminal offence since the Ottoman penal code of 1858 and transgender people have been able to change their legal gender since 1988 (with surgery, medical examination and court permission), but there is no comprehensive anti-discrimination law and same-sex marriage, civil unions and domestic partnerships are not recognised. Since 2015 authorities have banned Pride events in most years, and participants have faced police attacks; in ILGA-Europe's 2026 Rainbow Europe ranking Turkey placed 47th of 49 countries. In early 2026 Turkish media reported the government was considering legislation criminalising public advocacy of 'behaviour contrary to biological sex', a provision ultimately not included in that year's judicial reform package. The page records no Gaziantep-specific divergence, consistent with this record's assessment that a visibly trans visitor's exposure in the province is the national one, locally enforced.

Amnesty International's Türkiye report (Report 2025/26) documents the national enforcement climate that applies to provincial authorities in Gaziantep: in June 2025 authorities issued blanket bans against the LGBTI and Trans pride marches, police subjected peaceful protesters to unlawful use of force and over 90 people were arbitrarily detained; three activists were remanded in prison on 29 June 2025 under Law No. 2911 and released on 8 August pending trial, while prosecutions of 92 people for participating in pride marches continued at year's end. In December 2025 an İzmir court ordered the dissolution of the Young LGBTI+ Association, ruling it had shared 'obscene' images incompatible with 'society's moral values' that could 'encourage or promote' LGBTI identities. For Gaziantep this evidences the state-level hostility and case-by-case prosecutions under the same meeting-and-demonstrations law that a visibly trans visitor would face anywhere in Turkey, including this province.

flags: its governor is among the six provincial authorities documented as issuing bans on public LGBTI activities during the reporting year
